lessons.title: Pre-Money, Post-Money and Dilution Made Simple

children.text: An investor says: "We will put in ₹2 crore at a ₹10 crore valuation." Two founders hear that sentence and write down two different numbers. One thinks she is selling 20% of the company. The other thinks 16.67%. One word decides which is right, and that word is often left out of the conversation. This lesson gives you the four formulas that sit underneath every funding round, and enough practice that you can do the arithmetic in your head while the term sheet is still being discussed.

body.text: Valuation is not a measure of what your company is worth. It is a number the two sides agree to so the arithmetic of ownership can be settled. What matters is not the headline, it is the percentage that changes hands and the price per share that sets it.

children.text: The One Word That Changes Everything

markDefs.definition: The agreed value of the company before the new investment money comes in.
The value of the company immediately after the new money arrives: pre-money valuation plus the amount invested.

children.text: A
pre-money valuation
is what the company is agreed to be worth before the cheque lands. A
post-money valuation
includes the cheque. The money itself is now inside the company, sitting in its bank account, so the company really is worth more the moment it arrives.

body.caption: Every ownership calculation in a funding round starts here

body.title: The same ₹2 crore cheque, two readings of "₹10 crore valuation"

body.text: That single word is worth 3.33% of the company on a ₹2 crore round, and the gap widens as the cheque gets bigger. If an investor says "valuation" without saying pre or post, ask. If a term sheet says it ambiguously, get it written down clearly before anything else is negotiated.

body.title: Pre or post?
body.prompt: An angel invests ₹80 lakh at a ₹3.2 crore pre-money valuation. What percentage of the company does the angel own after the round? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Post-money is ₹3.2 crore + ₹0.8 crore = ₹4 crore. The angel's stake is ₹0.8 crore ÷ ₹4 crore = 20%. Had the ₹3.2 crore been quoted as post-money, the angel would have got ₹0.8 crore ÷ ₹3.2 crore = 25% instead, and the founders would have been 5 percentage points poorer.

children.text: From Percentages to Actual Shares
Percentages are the conversation, but shares are the paperwork. A company does not hand over a percentage, it issues new shares at a price. Two more formulas connect the two.

body.latex: \text{Price per share} = \frac{\text{Pre-money valuation}}{\text{Shares outstanding before the round}}
body.caption: The pre-money value is divided across the shares that already exist
The investor's money buys shares at that price

children.text: Take an illustrative Coimbatore company, LoomOS, with 10,00,000 shares held by its two founders. A seed fund invests ₹5 crore at a ₹20 crore pre-money valuation.

stats.label: Post-money
stats.context: ₹20 crore pre-money plus the ₹5 crore invested

body.caption: LoomOS cap table before and after the seed round

body.text: Look at what did not change. Both founders hold exactly the same number of shares after the round as before. Their percentages fell only because the denominator grew from 10,00,000 shares to 12,50,000. Dilution is division, not confiscation.

body.title: Work out the price per share
body.prompt: A startup has 8,00,000 shares outstanding. It raises ₹6 crore at a ₹24 crore pre-money valuation. What is the price per share, in rupees?
body.explanation: ₹24,00,00,000 ÷ 8,00,000 = ₹300 per share. The investor's ₹6 crore therefore buys ₹6,00,00,000 ÷ ₹300 = 2,00,000 new shares, taking the total to 10,00,000. The investor owns 2,00,000 ÷ 10,00,000 = 20%, which matches ₹6 crore ÷ ₹30 crore post-money.

children.text: Dilution Compounds Across Rounds

One round of dilution is easy to picture. Three rounds are where founders get surprised, because the effect multiplies rather than adds. Selling 20%, then 18%, then 15% does not leave you with 47%. It leaves you with what remains after each cut is taken from a progressively smaller slice.

body.latex: \text{Stake after a round} = \text{Stake before} \times (1 - \text{Share sold in the round})
body.caption: Apply this once per round, in order

body.title: Founders' combined ownership through three rounds (%)

children.text: The arithmetic: 100% × 0.80 = 80%, then 80% × 0.82 = 65.6%, then 65.6% × 0.85 = 55.76%. Three rounds, 53% of the total sold in headline terms, and the founders still hold a majority. Add an ESOP pool at each round, which Lesson 3.4 covers, and the number falls faster.

body.title: Three rounds of dilution
body.prompt: A founder starts with 100%. She sells 25% in a seed round, then 20% in a Series A, then 15% in a Series B. What percentage of the company does she hold after all three rounds? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 100% × 0.75 = 75%, then 75% × 0.80 = 60%, then 60% × 0.85 = 51%. Adding the sales together would wrongly suggest she gave away 60% and kept 40%. Dilution multiplies, so each round takes its cut from what is left, not from the original whole.

body.title: The trap hidden inside "pre-money": the option pool

children.text: There is a second question hiding behind every pre-money number: does the pre-money share count already include a new ESOP pool? It almost always does, and that quietly changes who pays for it.
Take a ₹5 crore investment at a ₹20 crore pre-money valuation, with the investor also asking for a 10% option pool.
Pool created pre-money:
the investor still gets 20%, the pool takes 10%, and the founders absorb the whole pool from their 80%, leaving them 70%.
Pool created post-money:
the 10% comes out of everyone, so the investor drops to 18%, the founders to 72%.

Two percentage points of a ₹25 crore company is ₹50 lakh of value, decided by a sentence most founders skim past. The market norm in India is a pre-money pool, so the practical negotiation is about the size of the pool, not its position. Argue it down with a hiring plan showing what grants you actually need over the next 18 months.
A Higher Valuation Is Not Automatically a Better Deal

body.caption: Two term sheets for the same company

cells: Bar set for the next round

children.text: Offer 2 has the bigger headline and is the worse deal. The larger option pool eats the founders' extra ownership, and a 2x participating liquidation preference means the investor takes ₹16 crore off the top at exit and then shares what is left. Lesson 4.2 unpacks those terms properly. The point here is that valuation is one line in a term sheet, not the scoreboard.

body.label: What a high valuation really costs
body.value: It sets the bar for the next round
body.context: Raise at ₹120 crore and your Series B has to be priced above that, which usually means growing three to four times before you run out of money. Miss it and you face a down round, which triggers anti-dilution clauses and damages morale far more than a modest valuation ever would.

body.title: Which statement is true?
body.question: A founder raises ₹4 crore at a ₹16 crore post-money valuation. Which of these statements is correct?
options: The company now has ₹16 crore in its bank account
The pre-money valuation was ₹16 crore and the investor owns 25%
The pre-money valuation was ₹12 crore and the investor owns 25%
The founder's remaining 75% is worth ₹16 crore
body.explanation: Post-money ₹16 crore minus the ₹4 crore invested gives a ₹12 crore pre-money valuation, and the investor's stake is ₹4 crore ÷ ₹16 crore = 25%. The bank holds ₹4 crore, not ₹16 crore, and the founder's 75% is worth ₹12 crore on paper at this price.

body.title: Negotiating the number that matters
body.scenario: Farhan is raising a seed round for his Ahmedabad logistics startup, which has 20,00,000 shares outstanding held by two founders. An investor offers ₹6 crore at a "₹24 crore valuation" and asks for a 12% ESOP pool. Farhan is delighted by the number and is about to say yes.
body.prompt: What must he clarify before agreeing, and what is his ownership under each interpretation?
body.modelAnswer:
Three questions before anything else.
1. Is ₹24 crore pre-money or post-money?
If pre-money: post is ₹30 crore, the investor gets ₹6 ÷ ₹30 = 20%, and price per share is ₹24 crore ÷ 20,00,000 = ₹120.
If post-money: pre is ₹18 crore, the investor gets ₹6 ÷ ₹24 = 25%, and price per share is ₹18 crore ÷ 20,00,000 = ₹90.
That one word costs 5 percentage points, or ₹1.5 crore of value at this price.
2. Is the 12% ESOP pool created before or after the money? Market practice in India is pre-money, meaning the founders absorb it. On the pre-money reading, the founders end up with roughly 100% − 20% − 12% = 68%, not 80%.
3. What instrument and what terms? A 20% stake through CCPS with a 1x non-participating preference is a very different deal from the same 20% with a 2x participating preference, as Lesson 4.2 shows.
What Farhan should do: get the term sheet to state pre-money explicitly, negotiate the pool down to what an honest 18-month hiring plan needs, perhaps 8%, and only then compare offers. A slightly lower valuation with a smaller pool and cleaner terms often leaves founders owning more and sleeping better.

body.title: The missing word
body.textWithBlank: If an investor quotes a valuation without saying whether it is pre-money or ___-money, the founder cannot calculate how much of the company is being sold.
body.explanation: Post-money equals pre-money plus the investment. The investor's stake is always the investment divided by the post-money valuation, so without knowing which number was quoted, the ownership split is undefined.

cards.definition: The agreed value of the company before the new investment arrives.
Pre-money valuation plus the amount invested. The investor's stake is always measured against this.
Pre-money valuation divided by the shares outstanding before the round.
The fall in an existing holder's percentage when new shares are issued. Share counts stay the same, the denominator grows.
An ESOP pool created before the investment, so existing shareholders rather than the new investor bear its dilution.
Your shares multiplied by the last round's price per share. It is not cash until someone buys those shares.

points: Post-money equals pre-money plus the investment, and the investor's stake is always investment divided by post-money.
The words pre and post are worth real money: ₹2 crore at ₹10 crore pre gives away 16.67%, at ₹10 crore post it gives away 20%.
Price per share is pre-money divided by existing shares. New shares issued is the investment divided by that price.
Dilution is division, not confiscation. Founders keep their share count and lose percentage as the denominator grows.
Dilution multiplies across rounds: selling 25%, then 20%, then 15% leaves the founder with 51%, not 40%.
A pre-money ESOP pool is paid for by existing shareholders, so negotiate its size against a real hiring plan.
A higher headline valuation with a bigger pool and harsher preferences is often the worse deal, and it raises the bar your next round must clear.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or financial advice. LoomOS, Farhan's company and all valuations, share counts and term sheet figures are illustrative and simplified: real rounds involve convertible instruments, multiple share classes and negotiated terms covered later in this course. Speak to a qualified professional before agreeing any funding terms.
